explanations.explanation: Gladness it is, friend. The psalm says, "Serve the LORD with gladness…" (Psalm 100:2). Service in this psalm isn't a chore you grit your teeth through. It comes with joyful songs right alongside it.

I get why fear came to mind, friend. Serving can feel heavy, like a batch you're sure you'll mess up. But the psalm says, "Serve the LORD with gladness…" (Psalm 100:2). Gladness is the word it uses, and joyful songs come right after it.

Patience is a good thing to have in a kitchen, friend. Believe me, I've waited on a lot of dough. But this psalm picks a different word: "Serve the LORD with gladness…" (Psalm 100:2). The service comes with joy and joyful songs.
Not quite, friend. The psalm doesn't say to tiptoe in. It says, "come into His presence with joyful songs." (Psalm 100:2). Songs are the opposite of sneaking in like you're late to a meeting.

False is right, friend. Nothing here says to slip in quietly. The text says, "come into His presence with joyful songs." (Psalm 100:2). It opens the whole psalm the same way with "Make a joyful noise to the LORD, all the earth." (Psalm 100:1).
That's it, baker. The psalm says, "It is He who made us, and we are His…" (Psalm 100:3). The One we're told to know as God is the One who made us. Nobody else gets the credit.

Abraham is a big name in the Bible, so I see the thinking, friend. But the psalm gives the credit somewhere else. It says, "Know that the LORD is God. It is He who made us…" (Psalm 100:3). The LORD made us.
Moses is a big name, friend, but he isn't named anywhere in this psalm. The psalm says, "Know that the LORD is God. It is He who made us…" (Psalm 100:3). The LORD is the one who made us.
True, baker. The psalm says, "It is He who made us, and we are His…" (Psalm 100:3). Made by Him and belonging to Him, both in one verse. It goes on to say "we are His people…"
The psalm says the opposite, friend. Right after saying who made us, it says, "…and we are His; we are His people…" (Psalm 100:3). It says it twice, back to back.
Sheep, yes! The psalm says, "we are His people, and the sheep of His pasture." (Psalm 100:3). It's a picture of belonging, with us as the ones in His pasture. I think it's a gentle picture.
Lions would make for a much louder pasture, friend! But the psalm says, "we are His people, and the sheep of His pasture." (Psalm 100:3). Sheep is the word the text uses.
Ravens would be a strange crowd for a pasture, friend. The psalm says, "we are His people, and the sheep of His pasture." (Psalm 100:3). Sheep is the picture it paints.
Right on, baker. The psalm says, "Enter His gates with thanksgiving and His courts with praise…" (Psalm 100:4). That's what you carry through the gate, a grateful heart and a song.

Gifts and sacrifices are a fair guess, friend, since gates and courts sound like that kind of place. But this psalm names something else: "Enter His gates with thanksgiving and His courts with praise…" (Psalm 100:4). Thanksgiving and praise are what it says to bring.

Not this time, friend. The psalm says, "Enter His gates with thanksgiving and His courts with praise…" (Psalm 100:4). Thanksgiving and praise are the words it uses. It's right in step with the joyful songs back in verse 2.

True, friend. The verse ends, "give thanks to Him and bless His name." (Psalm 100:4). Thanks and blessing go together at the close of that verse. So the psalm does tell people to bless the LORD's name.
It's actually in there, friend. Verse 4 ends, "give thanks to Him and bless His name." (Psalm 100:4). Blessing His name is part of the call, right next to giving thanks.
That's the reason, baker. The psalm says, "For the LORD is good, and His loving devotion endures forever…" (Psalm 100:5). All that noise and gladness and thanks comes from who He is.

A harvest would be a fine reason to celebrate, friend. But this psalm doesn't mention one. It says, "For the LORD is good, and His loving devotion endures forever…" (Psalm 100:5). His goodness is the reason it gives.

An enemy running off is a fair guess, friend, but this psalm doesn't mention one. The reason it gives is, "For the LORD is good, and His loving devotion endures forever…" (Psalm 100:5). His goodness is the reason.
Forever, baker! The psalm says, "…His loving devotion endures forever…" (Psalm 100:5). No expiration date, no best-by sticker. That's good news for a stamper who once had a price sticker of 25 cents.
Seventy years is a long stretch, friend, but the psalm goes way past that. It says, "…His loving devotion endures forever…" (Psalm 100:5). Forever is a lot longer than seventy.
That one adds a condition, friend, and the psalm doesn't. It says, "…His loving devotion endures forever…" (Psalm 100:5). It doesn't say forever unless something changes.
The psalm says much more than that, friend. It says, "His faithfulness continues to all generations." (Psalm 100:5). All generations is a whole lot more than one.
False is right, friend. The psalm says, "His faithfulness continues to all generations." (Psalm 100:5). That's not one generation, that's all of them, one after another.
